pi.name: Ann L. Miller
pi.title: Arthur F. Thurnau Professor of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology
pi.bio: Ann L. Miller earned a B.A. in Biochemistry from Gustavus Adolphus College and a Ph.D. in Molecular Biophysics and Biochemistry from Yale University in Tony Koleske's lab, then completed postdoctoral training in cell biology with Bill Bement at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. She joined the University of Michigan MCDB department as an Assistant Professor in 2011, was promoted to Associate Professor in 2018 and Professor in 2024, and was named an Arthur F. Thurnau Professor in 2025. She chaired the Signaling by Adhesion Receptors Gordon Research Conference in 2022 and has received the Class of 1923 Memorial Teaching Award (2018) and an Exceptional Mentor Award (2017). She also serves as MCDB's Community Engagement Faculty Liaison.

lab_description: The Miller Lab studies how epithelial cell-cell junctions maintain adhesion and barrier function while being dynamically remodeled during cell shape changes such as cytokinesis and morphogenesis. The lab uses Xenopus laevis embryos with live-cell imaging and quantitative microscopy to examine Rho GTPase regulation in space and time, actin cytoskeletal dynamics, and the roles of proteins including Anillin, MgcRacGAP, and Vinculin. Key discoveries include Rho flares, localized bursts of Rho activity that repair leaks in tight junctions, visualized with the lab's ZnUMBA barrier assay, and mechanosensitive recruitment of Vinculin to tricellular junctions. The lab also studies cortical excitability and cytokinesis using reconstituted systems of supported lipid bilayers and Xenopus egg extracts.

research_areas.title: Rho flares and tight junction repair
research_areas.summary: Localized Rho activation restores barrier function after junction breaches by concentrating tight junction proteins through actin polymerization and ROCK-mediated contraction, visualized with the lab's Zinc-based Ultrasensitive Microscopic Barrier Assay (ZnUMBA).

research_areas.title: Cell-cell junction remodeling during epithelial cytokinesis
research_areas.summary: Investigates how adhesion and barrier function persist as epithelial cells divide, including Vinculin-mediated stabilization of adherens junction proteins at the cleavage furrow and how neighbor cells restrain furrowing.

research_areas.title: Anillin in junctional and actomyosin regulation
research_areas.summary: The scaffolding protein Anillin regulates both junction integrity and cell mechanics; depletion reduces junctional F-actin while overexpression causes hypercontractility.

research_areas.title: Cortical pattern formation and excitability
research_areas.summary: Studies sustained waves of Rho activity and actin assembly using reconstituted supported lipid bilayers combined with Xenopus egg extracts imaged by TIRF microscopy.

research_areas.title: Cytokinesis regulation by Rho GTPase flux
research_areas.summary: Examines how RhoA activity zones form and focus the contractile ring during cell division, with emphasis on the regulatory role of MgcRacGAP.

joining: Postdoctoral applicants should email Dr. Ann Miller a cover letter explaining their interest in the lab and desired projects, a CV, and three references. Prospective graduate students apply through the MCDB department or the Program in Biomedical Sciences (PIBS); current graduate students interested in rotating should email Dr. Miller directly. Undergraduates are welcome for experience, for credit (BIO200, MCDB300, MCDB400), or for work study; the lab prefers sophomores so students can stay involved throughout college, but all may apply by emailing Dr. Miller.
